title: From Robots to Organizations: The Role of the AI Scientist

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Dementia is a growing health burden worldwide; however, scalable, low-cost strategies for early risk identification are lacking. Because cardiac and cognitive aging are closely associated, a routinely collected 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), interpreted using foundation model embeddings, is a promising and accessible candidate marker. However, it is unclear whether such embeddings carry predictive information independent of chronological age—the dominant risk factor for dementia—and whether the underlying changes follow a detectable prediagnostic trajectory. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to investigate whether foundation model embeddings of routine ECGs carry information that distinguishes patients later diagnosed with cognitive impairment or dementia from matched controls, beyond chronological age, and, if so, whether the underlying ECG changes intensify as diagnosis approaches. <strong>Methods:</strong> In a retrospective two-site Korean cohort (Severance Hospital, development n=52,355; Yongin Severance Hospital, external n=6500), embeddings from the knowledge-enhanced diagnosis foundation model supported an ECG-only classifier that discriminated patients diagnosed with cognitive impairment or dementia within the following 10 years from matched controls, using only ECGs interpreted as normal sinus rhythm. We compared an age-only model with a late fusion of age and ECG-derived probability and tested whether age-residualized embedding is predictive as direct evidence of age-independent information. Discrimination was summarized by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) with 95% bootstrap CIs, and DeLong tests and net reclassification improvement (NRI) were used for between-model comparisons. To trace the prediagnostic time course, we analyzed ECG phenotype labels across four windows before diagnosis in an exact-age-matched case-control set. <strong>Results:</strong> Chronological age strongly discriminated cases from controls in both cohorts (external AUROC 0.809, 95% CI 0.799-0.819). Adding ECG-derived probability improved discrimination, calibration, and net benefit over age alone (external AUROC 0.825, 95% CI 0.816-0.834; DeLong <i>P</i><.001; positive NRI). Critically, even after removing the age-predictable component, age-residualized embedding retained modest but reproducible discrimination in both internal (AUROC 0.590, 95% CI 0.581-0.599) and external (AUROC 0.579, 95% CI 0.567-0.592) validation (both <i>P</i><.001), indicating dementia-relevant information that was not explained by chronological age. Of the 105 ECG labels, 19 (18.1%) showed a case-control difference that widened significantly toward diagnosis, dominated by nonspecific ST segment and T wave changes, acute ischemic patterns (acute myocardial infarction), and atrial and junctional arrhythmias (atrial flutter, ectopic atrial, and accelerated junctional rhythms), with divergence emerging mainly in the proximal (1-3-year) and imminent (0-1-year) windows. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Routine ECG foundation model embeddings encode aging-related electrophysiological information that is complementary to and not fully explained by chronological age and intensifies as diagnosis approaches, with concurrent shifts toward ischemic and arrhythmic ECG patterns whose mechanism cannot be determined from these data. These findings suggest that routine ECG is a low-cost, age-complementary triage signal for cognitive impairment and dementia screening, rather than a stand-alone diagnostic test.
title: Electrocardiogram Embeddings Beyond Chronological Age for Prediagnostic Cognitive Impairment and Dementia: Development and External Validation Study

summary: The ethics of autonomous clinical AI are controversial. Traditional ethics assessments have focused on AI model performance rather than health system outcomes. Nichol and colleagues translate established research ethics principles into 9 practical recommendations for trials of autonomous clinical AI. Their findings support an evolution in clinical trial design. The accuracy and performance of the model is important, but the ethical unit of evaluation should be the complete care pathway, with prespecified obligations for subgroup performance, follow-up care, system failures, and model change.
title: The Ethics of Autonomous Clinical AI: Shifting From Model Accuracy to Model Impact

summary: Background: A central concern in ecological momentary assessment (EMA) research is whether repeated self-report alters the reporting process itself. In most EMA domains, longitudinal stability of reporting is assumed but rarely tested. Objective: This study leveraged concurrent accelerometry as a temporal anchor to evaluate (1) whether self-reported physical activity (PA) and sedentary behavior (SB) exhibited temporal shifts across a 7-day monitoring period and (2) whether this temporal shift differed across near-momentary (5-min reporting period) and coverage-based (120-min recall period) EMA protocols. Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of 315 US adults recruited from the Understanding America Study panel between January and July 2023 for the current study. Participants were monitored in their natural environments for 7 days via 2 measurement methods: continuous thigh-worn activPAL4 accelerometry and 5 daily smartphone EMA prompts assessing PA and SB. Reporting reactivity was defined as divergence in the temporal trajectories of EMA-reported behavior relative to accelerometry. Multilevel models with random intercepts and slopes tested whether linear and quadratic study day effects differed across the 2 methods (method × study day interactions). Protocol differences were examined using multivariable method × protocol × study day interactions, comparing coverage-based and near-momentary EMA designs. Results: In the coverage-based protocol, EMA-reported PA and SB exhibited temporal trajectories that diverged significantly from concurrent accelerometry (SB linear divergence: =1.40, 95% CI 0.20-2.61, =.02; PA linear divergence: =−1.91, 95% CI −2.93 to −0.90, <.001; and PA quadratic divergence: =0.28, 95% CI 0.12-0.44, <.001). No evidence of such divergence was found in the near-momentary protocol. The divergence in reporting trajectories differed significantly between the 2 protocols (SB linear 3-way interaction: =−2.58, =.02; PA linear 3-way interaction: =1.86, =.04). Conclusions: Reporting reactivity in EMA appears protocol-dependent. The coverage-based protocol was associated with modest reporting reactivity, which challenges the common assumption of reporting invariance in EMA and underscores the importance of considering protocol design when interpreting within-person change.
title: Temporal Stability of Repeated Self-Reported vs Device-Measured Behavior: Observational Study Using Ecological Momentary Assessment
Closing the Postpartum Gap With Reverse Call Centers Alongside Traditional Support Lines

summary: Background: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) has a rising global prevalence and brings short-term and long-term adverse risks for mothers and fetuses. Conventional in-person GDM care is limited by time and geographic barriers, often resulting in suboptimal compliance and delayed individualized interventions. Telemedicine is increasingly applied in GDM management; however, randomized controlled trial (RCT) evidence remains inconsistent. Objective: The study aims to pool data from RCTs to quantify the effects of telemedicine on glycemic control and pregnancy-related outcomes in women with GDM and to inform optimized clinical management. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Scopus up to August 16, 2026. Two reviewers independently performed study screening and data extraction. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2. Meta-analyses were conducted in Stata 18.0. For heterogeneous outcomes, 95% prediction intervals (PIs) were calculated to estimate effect ranges for future studies. Heterogeneity was explored via leave-one-out sensitivity, meta-regression, and subgroup analyses. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) framework rated evidence certainty. Publication bias was evaluated for outcomes reported in ≥10 studies. Results: Twenty-three RCTs (3055 women with GDM) were included. Pooled estimates suggested that telemedicine may reduce fasting glucose (mean difference [MD] −0.26, 95% CI −0.42 to −0.09, 95% PI −0.93 to 0.42; =.002), 2-hour postprandial glucose (MD −0.50, 95% CI −0.87 to −0.14, 95% PI −1.84 to 0.84; =.007), and gestational weight gain (MD −0.78, 95% CI −1.40 to −0.17, 95% PI −2.83 to 1.26; =.01). Telemedicine was also associated with lower risks of cesarean section, emergency cesarean section, macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, and neonatal respiratory distress. No significant differences were found for hemoglobin A, preterm birth, or neonatal intensive care unit admission. Notably, fasting glucose, 2-hour postprandial glucose, and gestational weight gain exhibited very high unexplained heterogeneity (²>90%), with their 95% PIs crossing the null value despite statistically significant pooled effects. The GRADE certainty of evidence was very low to low across all assessed outcomes. Conclusions: Telemedicine may improve selected glycemic and perinatal outcomes for women with GDM and may serve as a promising supplementary option for prenatal care, particularly in resource-limited settings where routine in-person follow-up is difficult to implement. Nevertheless, the apparent benefits for glycemic control and gestational weight gain remain tentative due to extreme, unexplained between-study heterogeneity and 95% PIs crossing the null. Based on current evidence, telemedicine should not completely replace standard antenatal care. Future well-designed, large-sample RCTs are warranted; such trials should adopt standardized definitions for telemedicine interventions, fully report intervention components, and conduct long-term follow-up to verify sustained maternal and neonatal clinical benefits. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420261403669; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261403669
title: The Impact of Telemedicine Interventions on Maternal and Fetal Outcomes in Women With Gestational Diabetes: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

summary: Over the last 2 decades, a large global marketplace has emerged in which businesses use direct-to-consumer advertising to sell putative stem cell treatments that are unsupported by convincing scientific evidence of safety and efficacy. It is common for such purported stem cell therapies not to have been reviewed and approved by national regulatory authorities, even though they are supposed to undergo rigorous premarketing review by regulatory bodies responsible for evaluating such medical products and determining whether they are backed by sufficient evidence to warrant approval. The marketing claims, commercial activities, and clinical practices of such businesses have resulted in patients experiencing serious harms, including loss of life, physical injuries, financial losses, and avoidable delays in accessing evidence-based treatments. Such businesses are also responsible for collective harms, including diverting patients from participating in legitimate stem cell clinical studies, damaging the field of credible stem cell research, and contributing to public confusion and misunderstandings about how to distinguish evidence-based stem cell therapies from stem cell interventions that are not backed by robust data. Researchers in bioethics, health law, the social sciences, and other academic fields have made important contributions to the critical analysis of direct-to-consumer digital marketing claims made by businesses selling unproven and unapproved stem cell interventions. Scholars studying such marketing representations have documented the use of persuasive “tokens of legitimacy” to make advertised stem cell interventions seem credible, trustworthy, and backed by current scientific evidence. Acknowledging the value of such scholarship, there is a growing need for the development of best practices in research methods and data-archiving practices. In particular, there is a need for increased digital archiving of online marketing claims made by businesses selling supposed stem cell treatments. Numerous parties can benefit from increased digital archiving of such problematic marketing representations. However, analyzing, archiving, and critiquing the marketing claims, business operations, and clinical practices of such businesses must be done in a careful, rigorous, and evidence-based manner that is attentive to the intimidating tactics some of these businesses use when responding to public criticism. Researchers need to document the marketing representations made by businesses selling unapproved and unproven stem cell interventions in ways that minimize exposure to legal threats and other efforts to suppress critical analysis. Using the Wayback Machine or other comparable archiving tools to create digital repositories of such marketing representations is one way to mitigate such threats, by capturing the exact claims such businesses make when promoting putative stem cell therapies. Archiving such digital marketing representations is important for academic research and can play a valuable role in other contexts, such as in legal actions taken against businesses using purportedly deceptive marketing claims to sell unproven and unapproved stem cell-based interventions.
title: Digital Archiving of Direct-to-Consumer Marketing Claims Made by Businesses Selling Unproven Stem Cell Interventions

summary: Human trials in dietary and cosmetic domains generate large volumes of multimodal data but remain limited in their ability to produce integrated and actionable insights. Data such as intake records, physiological biomarkers, imaging outputs, and user-reported outcomes are typically collected through disconnected systems and analyzed independently, restricting the ability to establish time-resolved relationships between exposure and response. In this viewpoint, we define this limitation as the AI transformation (AX) gap, representing a structural disconnect between data generation and actionable knowledge in human trials. Drawing on evidence from real-world industry demand, we highlight how this gap is consistently observed across dietary intervention trials, cosmetic human trials, and underlying data systems. We propose a conceptual AX-driven framework that integrates multimodal data acquisition, continuously aligns intervention exposure with corresponding physiological, phenotypic, and participant-reported responses across time, and supports centralized analytical processing. The framework is intended to provide a unified perspective for transforming fragmented human-trial data into integrated, interpretable, and actionable knowledge. Although the proposed framework has not yet been empirically validated, it offers a conceptual foundation for future development and evaluation of integrated data platforms in dietary intervention and cosmetic human trials. Closing the AX gap may facilitate the transition from fragmented data collection toward human trials in which multimodal exposure and response data are continuously linked across time to support more integrated and individualized interpretation in research and product development.
title: Data-Rich But Integration-Poor Human Trials: Conceptual Framework for Closing the AI Transformation Gap in Dietary Intervention and Cosmetic Human Trials

summary: Background: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a chronic condition that requires ongoing self-management. While chatbots offer scalable monitoring and management, evidence on their integration into structured hospital tele-support workflows, where patient engagement and digital readiness may differ from those in standalone digital interventions, remains limited. Objective: This study aimed to describe the design of a clinical protocol–guided chatbot, Sharing Information with Users on Diabetes Actions and Interventions (), and evaluate its feasibility, usability, and acceptability among patients and telecarers within a hospital tele-support program. Methods: We used an embedded mixed methods design (QUAL [quan]) guided by the World Health Organization (WHO) monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions and the theoretical framework of acceptability. Through a co-design process involving clinicians, researchers, telecarers, and developers, the chatbot was aligned with established clinical protocols. It featured 7 precall sessions designed to collect patient data, generate summary reports for staff, and deliver targeted educational content. Patients (≥21-year-old individuals with T2DM) and telecarer nurses (with experience ≥6 mo) were recruited from an existing tele-support program. Data sources included interviews, online surveys (5-point Likert scale), and chatbot usage logs. Qualitative data were analyzed thematically; quantitative data were summarized descriptively to supplement and contextualize the qualitative findings. Results: Fourteen participants (7 patients and 7 telecarers) completed both interviews and surveys and were included in the analysis. Patients (mean age 45.3, SD 15.4 y) had a median diabetes duration of 10 (IQR 3-25; range 1‐30) years, and all were digitally literate. Telecarers had a median of 5 (IQR 4-9) years of telehealth experience. Quantitatively, patients showed high engagement, completing 79% of started sessions with a median completion time of 2 minutes and 58 seconds. Patient satisfaction was high, with 86% (6/7) willing to recommend the tool; however, telecarer endorsement for universal rollout to patients in other clinical programs or outpatient clinics was more cautious (3/7, 43%). Qualitative findings revealed 5 themes: (1) perceptions of chatbot usability, (2) alignment and integration into telecarers’ processes, (3) factors influencing acceptability of the chatbot, (4) perceived efficacy of the chatbot for T2DM self-management and care delivery, and (5) suggested improvements and enhancements. Integrated findings revealed that the chatbot was usable and functioned as a precall support tool that optimized the personalization of tele-support sessions. However, its perceived efficacy in self-management behavior was limited by this cohort’s extensive experience with T2DM management. Key barriers to adoption included administrative burden for telecarers due to a lack of electronic medical record integration and content redundancy for patients. Suggested enhancements included multilingual support and adaptive content catering to different levels of disease-specific literacy. Conclusions: A clinical protocol–guided chatbot is feasible for hospital tele-support, complementing rather than replacing human care. It automates routine assessments and reinforces education, but future iterations must prioritize workflow integration and adaptive content to sustain engagement.
title: Evaluation of a Clinical Protocol–Guided Chatbot to Support Telecarers in Diabetes Management: Embedded Mixed Methods Study

summary: In recent years, remote exercise services (“telerehabilitation”) have been increasingly explored and implemented, including in supportive cancer care, on the promise of greater convenience, access independent of geographic location, reduced infection risk, and cost savings. Ethical commentary on telehealth in general is substantial, but sustained discussion of questions specific to telerehabilitation remains comparatively sparse. As contributors to PREFERBALE-II, a European Union–funded project evaluating live-remote exercise for people recovering from cancer treatment, we sought practical guidance on how to deliver such services responsibly, and found little to work with. This prompted this viewpoint, which sets out our own position as researchers and clinicians engaged in this work. We draw on a purposive sample of professional guidance documents, which were assembled through our professional networks and a supplementary web search, and on a narrative reading of qualitative studies chosen to represent accounts of benefits as well as burdens. We read these documents through an analytical lens of responsible innovation. We make 3 arguments. First, the ethical content of current telerehabilitation guidance is largely confined to the products and processes of innovation, covering safety, privacy, consent, and compliance, while the question of purpose, that is, whether, for whom, and why remote rehabilitation should be offered at all, is left largely unasked. Anticipation appears only implicitly, and reflexivity, inclusion, and responsiveness barely at all. Responsibility is repeatedly delegated to individual professionals without commensurate structural support. Second, the situated experience of users and professionals forms part of the ethics of telerehabilitation and is not merely data to be assessed. Reported benefits and burdens depend on social context, including age, digital literacy, connectivity, caregiver availability, language, and sensory or cognitive impairment, so an equity claim made for the modality in general may not hold for the individual patient. Third, the ethics of telerehabilitation consequently has to be institutionalized across 3 overlapping domains: the interpersonal and experiential quality of remote care, the legal and institutional conditions of delivery, and the positioning of telerehabilitation within health systems. We address these arguments primarily to rehabilitation professionals and the associations and standard-setting bodies that issue guidance for them, and secondarily to digital health and ethical, legal, and social implications researchers, policymakers, and health-system decision-makers who commission or implement such services. We offer an agenda for a broader ethics conversation across professional societies, curricula, and affected publics, together with observations from a consortium put forward as hypotheses for study.
title: Ethics of Telerehabilitation in Supportive Cancer Care Through a Responsible Innovation Lens
